title: Automated Privilege Logging
answer: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify, describe and list documents withheld from production in litigation because they are protected by attorney client privilege or the work product doctrine. It sits inside e-discovery, where a privilege log is a required disclosure in most civil matters and a frequent source of disputes over completeness and specificity. The work covers the whole withheld set, not just the obvious lawyer emails, and it has to produce an entry a court will accept for each item.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify, describe and list documents withheld from production in litigation because they are protected by attorney client privilege or the work product doctrine. It sits inside e-discovery, where a privilege log is a required disclosure in most civil matters and a frequent source of disputes over completeness and specificity. The work covers the whole withheld set, not just the obvious lawyer emails, and it has to produce an entry a court will accept for each item.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the same review platforms that host the rest of the matter, with the documents, metadata and coding fields held in one system so the log can be generated from the review database rather than rebuilt by hand. Privilege logging tools sit alongside technology assisted review and analytics, and they draw on the extracted text, email threads and participant roles already in the platform. Output is usually a spreadsheet or a load file that can be produced to opposing counsel and filed with the court.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach is to train or configure a classifier on documents already coded as privileged, then use it to rank the remaining set so reviewers see the likely privileged material first. The software can also assemble draft log entries from metadata, such as author, recipient, date and document type, and from the privilege basis recorded by the reviewer. Human review remains the step that confirms the claim and writes the description, because the log is a sworn statement about each document. Sampling and quality checks on the generated entries are standard practice before the log is served.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The log itself is a representation to the court and to the other side, so accuracy matters more than speed, and an overbroad or vague entry invites a challenge that can waive protection. Courts have grown less tolerant of logs that simply repeat boilerplate categories, and several decisions have addressed how much detail is enough. Where a tool drafts entries, the firm still owns the claim, and the review record should show who checked what. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents and 229 compliance and regulation pages, which is a reminder that privilege practice is shaped by rulings and rules rather than by the software alone.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward logs generated as a by product of review, with entries drafted from the coding decisions and metadata rather than compiled in a separate pass at the end. Better classification of privilege and work product, and better handling of family relationships and thread structure, are the areas where the tools are improving. Courts are likely to keep pressing on specificity, which pushes firms toward richer descriptions and clearer records of the basis for each withholding. The site currently tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and privilege questions in those matters will keep feeding back into how these tools are built and used.
